core: A variable is a named binding to a value (an identifier associated with an object/value in memory)
Declaration vs assignment vs use of a variable
A variable's value can change over time through reassignment (rebinding the name)
Identifier/naming rules and conventions for good names
The 'labeled box' mental model and its limits: a variable is a name bound to a value, not a physical container; reassignment rebinds the name; some languages distinguish value vs reference/aliasing
supporting: Immutable vs mutable values as it affects what reassignment does
Language differences: keywords for declaration (var/let/const) vs dynamic binding in Python
outOfScope: Data types in depth (own topic: data-types) — only note that a variable has/holds a value of some type
Scope in depth (own topic: scope) — only note that a name is valid within a region

claims.claim: In Python, names refer to objects and are introduced by name-binding operations; assignment is one such binding operation.
Assignment statements (re)bind names to values; if a name is already bound, assignment rebinds it to the new object.
A variable is a name that refers to a value; an assignment statement creates a variable and gives it a value.
Identifiers may contain letters, digits, and underscores, cannot begin with a digit, are case sensitive, and cannot be reserved keywords (e.g., Python: if, def, class, return).

In some languages declaring a variable and assigning it a value are distinct steps: in JavaScript `let x` is a declaration and `= 42` is an initializer, and a declared-but-uninitialized variable holds `undefined`.

Immutable objects (numbers, strings, tuples in Python) cannot be altered in place; storing a different value requires creating a new object, so reassigning a name bound to an immutable value binds it to a new object.
Two names can be bound to the same (mutable) object, so mutating through one name is visible through the other; rebinding one name does not affect the other.
A namespace is where names are stored (the place a variable is stored); binding a name at module level makes it a global variable, and within a function makes it a local variable.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a variable 'contains' its value (box model) or 'refers to' its value (name-binding model).
positions: Beginner texts often say a variable is a box that stores a value.
Python's model is that a name is bound to an object; the name refers to the value rather than containing it.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the box as a starting intuition and then states its limits explicitly: reassignment rebinds a name, and two names can share one object. The name-binding description is the more accurate one and is used for the technical claims.

sourceRecords.title: The Python Language Reference — Simple statements (assignment statements)
sourceRecords.notes: States assignment statements '(re)bind names to values' and that 'the name is rebound if it was already bound.' Supports declaration/assignment, reassignment/rebinding, and value-changes-over-time claims. Read directly.

sourceRecords.title: The Python Language Reference — Lexical analysis (identifiers and keywords)
sourceRecords.notes: Identifier grammar: name_start is letters/underscore/non-ASCII, name_continue adds digits; identifiers are any NAME except keywords; case is significant; keyword list includes if/def/class/return. Supports naming-rules claim. Read directly.

sourceRecords.notes: immutable = 'An object with a fixed value ... a new object has to be created if a different value has to be stored'; namespace = 'the place where a variable is stored.' Supports immutable-vs-mutable effect of reassignment and namespace note. Read directly.
